sections.overview: The western honey bee is a social insect whose colony functions through cooperation among thousands of females and a smaller number of males. Its natural range spans Africa, Europe and western Asia, while people have transported managed colonies widely for honey and crop pollination. Wild colonies still nest independently in some regions, so the species cannot be described only as a domesticated hive animal.
sections.identification: Adults have a hairy thorax, a banded abdomen and two pairs of wings joined by tiny hooks in flight. Worker females are usually about 10–15 millimetres long, drones about 15–17 millimetres, and egg-laying queens roughly 18–20 millimetres; these are indicative caste ranges, not fixed limits. A worker’s hind-leg pollen basket, or corbicula, and its branched body hairs help carry pollen, while the male’s very large eyes aid aerial mate-searching. Workers are about 10–15 mm long and queens about 18–20 mm; a reliable general adult body-mass range by caste was not found in the consulted sources.
sections.habitat: Colonies need repeated access to flowering plants, water and a protected nesting cavity; hollow trees are natural nest sites, and buildings or managed hives can provide alternatives. The species uses meadows, open woodland, gardens and agricultural landscapes, and may persist in drier or wetter settings where forage and shelter remain available.
sections.diet: Foragers use a long proboscis to drink floral nectar, carrying it in a crop separate from the digestive midgut; pollen is packed into hind-leg baskets and supplies protein, lipids and micronutrients. Nectar fuels adult flight, while digested pollen supplies nurse bees with nutrients used by their head glands to produce larval food. Nestmates receive incoming nectar, add glandular enzymes, pass it among workers and fan air over it as water evaporates, turning the sugary liquid into stored honey. Pollen mixed with nectar and salivary secretions becomes bee bread in comb cells, and stored honey fuels the colony when flowers are scarce.
sections.behavior: A colony is eusocial: queens reproduce, workers normally do not, and drones mate with queens from other colonies. Worker jobs commonly shift with age from cleaning cells and feeding brood to building wax comb, guarding entrances and foraging, although workers can change tasks when the colony loses bees or brood. Pheromones and food-sharing coordinate the colony’s tasks. Workers fan air or vibrate flight muscles to hold the brood nest near 34 degrees Celsius. Returning foragers may perform a waggle dance: its angle relative to vertical signals direction relative to the sun, and the waggle-run duration roughly indicates distance.
sections.reproduction: Usually, unfertilized eggs develop as haploid males, with one chromosome set, and fertilized eggs as diploid females, with two sets; rarely, a fertilized egg carrying two identical variants of the sex-determining gene csd develops as a diploid male, which workers generally destroy early. Larval nutrition helps determine whether a female becomes a worker or queen. Workers rear queens in enlarged cells, feeding them royal jelly throughout development; worker larvae receive nurse-produced brood food that changes with age and includes honey- and pollen-derived nutrients. After emerging, a virgin queen takes orientation flights and mates in flight with several drones at congregation areas, storing sperm for later egg fertilization; drones die after successful mating. Egg-to-adult development usually takes about 16 days for queens, 21 for workers and 24 for drones, though temperature affects timing. In a seasonal colony, swarming is colony-level reproduction: the old queen and many workers leave to establish a nest elsewhere while a successor queen develops.
sections.ecology: When workers visit flowers for nectar and pollen, grains stick to their hairy bodies and can reach stigmas on later visits, making the bee an important pollinator of wild plants and crops. Wild insects can improve crop fruit set even where honey bees visit flowers, so managed colonies do not replace diverse pollinator communities. Where managed colonies are dense and forage is limited, honey bees can compete with wild bees for nectar and pollen; studies find variable outcomes, and many have measured visitation or resource overlap rather than lasting population effects. Shared pathogens are another possible route of impact, so ecological effects depend on local colony density, resources and species.
sections.conservation: Conservation assessments distinguish self-sustaining wild colonies from human-managed hives. In 2025, IUCN classified wild colonies in the 27 European Union member states as Endangered, based on estimated decline and evidence of threats. The wider pan-European status remains Data Deficient because distribution, survival and trend data are sparse; the 2014 European assessment was also Data Deficient. Threats cited for wild honey bees include parasites, pests, predators, pathogens, pesticides and hybridization. Across European wild pollinators, IUCN also identifies habitat loss, intensive farming, fragmentation, nitrogen deposition and pesticides as pressures.
